evals.prompt: I run platform partnerships at Calvetta, a B2B scheduling and ops SaaS with around 900 mid-market customers. We have 310 free connectors in our integrations directory today and we take nothing on any of them. Leadership wants paid apps live by Q2 and told me "take 20%, maybe 25%, we'll land on it later, just go build the billing." Nothing else has been decided. Write me the monetization design.
evals.expected_output: A run that refuses to invent the take-rate, routes the level/tier decision to the strategy layer, fixes merchant-of-record posture as the first decision, notes developer-billed is the right default only while the rate is zero and states the promotion condition, and runs the interview one question at a time including the deadline, durability and effort-ceiling questions.
expectations: States that the take-rate level and tier architecture is not decided by this design and must be settled first
Names samber/developer-platform-skills@connector-marketplace-strategy as where the take-rate level and tier decision belongs
Does not adopt, endorse, or build the design around 20% or 25% as the rate
Identifies the merchant-of-record posture as the first decision, from which tax liability, chargeback ownership, offerable pricing models, and payouts all follow
States that while the take-rate is zero the default posture is developer-billed (vendor-as-MoR), because there is no cut to collect and collection machinery buys nothing
States the promotion condition explicitly: the moment a non-zero take-rate is charged, promote to marketplace-billed (platform-as-MoR)
Justifies marketplace-billed by collection at source being the only mechanism that does not depend on developer self-reporting
Asks interview questions one at a time rather than delivering a batch list or assuming the answers
Asks whether Calvetta already bills these end customers on a recurring invoice or settlement cycle for its core product
Asks the hard-date, one-off-unlock-versus-compounding-asset, and effort-ceiling questions, and states that a hard date promotes managed rails and the simplest posture
Sequences the work so the merchant-of-record posture is validated before the fee stack, payout design, and tax map are drafted

evals.prompt: Quick sanity check. We're a B2B data-quality platform, our app marketplace launches next month, and we've settled on developer-billed: each app vendor charges the customer directly on their own processor and we invoice them our 12% quarterly based on what they report. So tax is entirely theirs, right? For context, buyers sit in 22 US states and five EU countries, and roughly 12% of our seats go to one-person consultancies buying as individuals. I want one line in the developer agreement saying vendors are responsible for all taxes.
evals.expected_output: A run that answers no, explains that facilitator and deemed-supplier obligations attach by law regardless of billing posture, replaces the blanket clause with a published jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction split, separates tax status from card-network merchant of record, routes through counsel, and flags the self-reported 12% as the weakest enforcement position.
expectations: Answers no: marketplace-facilitator and deemed-supplier obligations can attach to the platform by law regardless of who bills the customer
Names US marketplace-facilitator statutes and ties them to the 2018 South Dakota v. Wayfair economic-nexus decision
States the US facilitator framework is state-by-state rather than federal, with variations such as excluded local taxes or continuing seller informational returns
Names the EU deemed-supplier rule (Article 14a of the e-commerce VAT package, in force since 1 July 2021) treating the electronic interface as having bought and resold the supply
States the EU deemed-supplier rule attaches to B2C supplies specifically, making the individual-buyer share a tax-design input rather than demographic trivia
Notes B2B cross-border EU supplies are typically reverse-charged to the business buyer, so the business-buyer portion is a lighter version of the layer, not an exemption
Rejects the single blanket clause that vendors are responsible for all taxes as the deliverable
Specifies the deliverable as a published split naming which tax, which jurisdiction, and whose obligation, rather than a binary toggle
States that marketplace-facilitator or deemed-supplier status is tax law while merchant of record is card-network status, and that the two are legally distinct and do not always coincide
Warns that marketplace sales may still count toward a seller's own nexus thresholds or filing obligations even where a platform remits
States this is not tax advice and routes the published split through qualified counsel before shipping
Flags that collecting 12% from developer-reported figures means the platform learns its own revenue from the payer, and pairs it with an anti-circumvention rule backed by a delisting path

evals.prompt: Engineering question on our marketplace build. We're on Stripe Connect. The plan: destination charges so our name is on the customer's statement, losses_collector set to stripe so we aren't eating chargebacks, full Stripe dashboards for each app vendor so they can self-serve refunds and see their own data, and we hold every sale 45 days before releasing the vendor's share. Platform fee comes out via application_fee_amount. Anything we should tighten before we ship?
evals.expected_output: A run that rejects the à-la-carte dial combination, explains that non-direct charge patterns require the platform to carry losses, names the two coherent bundles, states destination charges cannot implement a 45-day hold and that separate charges and transfers are required, warns off on_behalf_of, and raises per-active-developer rail costs.
expectations: Flags the combination as invalid: a non-direct charge pattern requires the platform to carry losses, so destination charges with Stripe as loss collector is blocked or silently shifts liability back to the platform
States the account dials (dashboard access, fee collection, loss liability) collapse into two coherent bundles rather than being freely mixable
Names the marketplace-shaped bundle: express dashboard, platform collects fees, platform carries losses, destination or separate charges
Names the SaaS-shaped bundle: full dashboard, Stripe bills the developer, Stripe carries losses, direct charges only
Flags full-dashboard access as belonging to the SaaS-shaped bundle and inconsistent with the destination-charge, platform-as-MoR intent
States destination charges pay the connected account on payment success and therefore cannot implement a hold-and-release model
Prescribes separate charges and transfers as the pattern required for delayed, gated, or split payouts
States the charge pattern is what technically determines merchant of record: direct charges make the developer MoR, destination and separate charges make the platform MoR
Warns against using on_behalf_of for marketplace use cases because it keeps the charge on the platform while making the developer merchant of record
Instructs picking a whole bundle rather than dials à la carte, naming the failure mode as the platform carrying dispute losses it believed it had pushed to developers
Requires the 45-day hold to be sized against actual refund and chargeback exposure and published as part of an end-to-end sale-to-bank timeline

Raises the per-active-developer cost of the managed marketplace bundle (per-account monthly fee plus fixed and percentage per-payout fees on top of processing) and says to model unit economics per active developer, not per transaction

evals.prompt: We publish our marketplace pricing-model menu to partners on Monday. The launch deck promises vendors can sell flat subscriptions, per-seat, metered usage, and one-time add-ons. Our checkout is the one that shipped with our commerce vendor: it does subscriptions and one-time purchases, plus coupons and free trials. Our head of partnerships also wants every vendor forced to offer a 14-day free trial, and we were going to list each plan as price variants under a single product so the catalog stays tidy. Sanity-check the plan.
evals.expected_output: A run that blocks the metered promise until the checkout is verified, states the rails cap the menu rather than the reverse, notes platform-as-MoR does not itself rule out metered billing, rejects price-variants-under-one-product and the mandated trial, and names the entitlement and reporting systems left unspecified.
expectations: Blocks publishing metered or usage-based pricing until the checkout is confirmed to support it
States the rails cap the pricing menu rather than the menu driving the rails choice
Identifies the promised metered tier as unsupported by the described checkout and requires either removing it from Monday's menu or changing the rails first
States the verification order explicitly: verify each promised model against the rails before publishing the menu to developers
Notes that a marketplace-billed posture does not by itself rule out usage-based billing, citing a platform-as-merchant-of-record marketplace that supports metered billing natively
Treats usage-based pricing as a maturity ladder (simple metering versus dimensional, contract-grade metering) and scopes which rung vendors actually need
Rejects modeling plan tiers as price variants of one product and requires each tier to be modeled as its own product object
Gives the reason: variants of one product become indistinguishable on customer invoices
Rejects mandating the 14-day free trial, and recommends the marketplace recommend defaults such as trials or an entry plan rather than mandate them
States the pricing-model menu is deliberately unranked because developer demand and rails capability decide it jointly
Notes a monetization stack is at least three systems (payment, entitlement or licensing provisioning, and partner revenue reporting) and that the checkout decision leaves the other two unspecified

evals.prompt: Designing our small-developer fee waiver. Draft: any app vendor whose marketplace revenue stayed under $400,000 in the trailing 12 months pays 0% instead of our 15%. Vendors apply via a form in the partner portal, our partner-ops person reviews applications once a quarter, and approved waivers start the following quarter. Vendors running several apps under different company entities each get their own $400K allowance. Tear it apart.
evals.expected_output: A run that identifies the manual-enrollment defect and requires defaulting eligible developers in, challenges the threshold against the ~$1M cluster, forces an explicit annual-reset-versus-lifetime decision, closes the separate-entity aggregation gap, and specifies mid-period crossing behavior.
expectations: Flags the application-and-review enrollment as the core defect: eligible developers who miss the paperwork silently pay the full rate
Requires defaulting eligible developers into the waiver automatically rather than making them opt in
States the reason: an opt-in waiver changes paper rather than behavior
Challenges the $400,000 threshold against the roughly $1M revenue threshold that major marketplace waiver programs cluster around, and recommends anchoring there rather than inventing a number
Names annual-reset versus lifetime cap as an explicit design decision to make rather than a detail
Notes that moving from an annual reset to a lifetime cap is a one-way tightening
Flags the per-entity allowance as a gap and requires associated or affiliated accounts to aggregate toward the cap
Requires a stated rule for what happens when a vendor crosses the threshold mid-period
Classifies the draft as a revenue-exemption tier and identifies that shape as the default waiver rung on efficiency grounds
States that fee waivers are a standard menu item across major marketplaces rather than an exceptional discount
Names waiver coverage among eligible developers as the post-launch metric proving the default-in rule worked, and pairs the waiver with a published notice commitment for later changes

evals.prompt: Our developer docs currently say "payouts are issued monthly, $25 minimum." Partners keep telling us cash flow is painful. We want to fix it by dropping the minimum to $10 and adding a line saying most partners get paid within 30 days. What actually happens: we close the month, run a 30-day refund window, the finance batch goes out on the 15th of the following month, and international wires take another 3 to 5 days. We're merchant of record and we bill customers in seven currencies.
evals.expected_output: A run that identifies the hold window rather than the minimum as the real cash-flow lever, computes the honest end-to-end lag and rejects the 30-day claim, offers rolling-with-reserves as the promotion and instant-for-a-fee only as a layered option, and assigns cross-border FX and rail choice to the platform.
expectations: Identifies the minimum payout threshold as the wrong lever and the hold window as the one developers actually feel
States that marketplace payout minimums cluster in roughly the $50 to $150 range, small enough that active developers clear them every cycle, so moving $25 to $10 changes little
States the real end-to-end sale-to-bank lag for a sale made early in a month runs well past 60 days once month close, the 30-day window, the mid-month batch, and wire time stack
Rejects publishing "most partners get paid within 30 days" as inaccurate against the described sequence
Requires publishing the honest end-to-end sale-to-bank timeline in the developer docs
Identifies the current design as the monthly-cycle-plus-explicit-hold-window rung and sizes the hold to actual refund and chargeback exposure, noting roughly 30 to 60 days as the platform norm
Offers rolling payouts with reserves, a percentage held on a rolling window against disputes, as the promotion when competing for supply against faster-paying alternatives
Offers instant payout for a fee only as an option layered on a slower default, never as the default, because it loses every round on operator risk and cost
Raises invoice-cycle consolidation only on the precondition that the platform already bills these customers on an existing settlement cycle

States that under the marketplace-billed posture the platform owns cross-border mechanics including payout currency conversion and payment-rail choice across the seven currencies, and says to budget it
Adds median sale-to-bank days measured against the published timeline as a tracked post-launch metric

evals.prompt: Two things. First, the fee schedule: we want partners to see one clean number, 18% all-in with our card-processing cost folded inside it, plus a $2,500 fee per app submission. Second, our second-largest app, 190 installs, has started putting a "pay here instead" link in their in-app onboarding that routes billing to their own checkout. Our partner agreement says nothing about it. How do we handle both?
evals.expected_output: A run that unbundles processing from the headline share as a separately labeled pass-through, names netting at source as the collection mechanism, separates the flat instruments, treats the external billing link as a terms violation needing an anti-circumvention rule plus delisting path, and commits a written notice period for fee changes.
expectations: Rejects folding payment-processing cost into the headline share and requires it as a separately labeled pass-through line
Gives the reason: a share that silently includes processing reads as a higher take than it is and cannot be compared honestly against competitors' headline rates
Names revenue share netted at source as the collection mechanism, deducted before payout rather than invoiced, audited, or chased
Evaluates the $2,500 submission fee against the real cost it funds, such as the security or app review, rather than accepting it as a round number
Notes that a registration-style flat fee should be sized to deter low-intent or spam submissions without deterring legitimate developers
Distinguishes one-time registration fees, per-app review fees, and annual listing fees as separate flat instruments rather than one undifferentiated charge
Treats the "pay here instead" link as circumvention of the revenue share and a partner-terms violation, not a pricing complaint or a product decision
Requires writing an explicit anti-circumvention rule into the partner terms
Requires backing that rule with a delisting path, stating that a rule without a removal path is only a preference
Notes that circumvention pressure rises with the take-rate

Requires a written, committed notice period for fee changes, roughly six months as the established pattern, published alongside the fee schedule, with unfavorable changes deferred and favorable ones accelerated

evals.prompt: Final review before we flip the switch in three weeks. Recap: we're merchant of record, 15% rev share netted out before payout, automatic tax calculation is switched on in our billing provider for all 50 US states and the EU, we have 40 active app vendors averaging about $600 a month gross each, monthly payouts, and a $1M annual exemption tier. Our ops dashboard will watch payout volume and take revenue. What would you check?
evals.expected_output: A run that flags the silent zero-tax failure and demands registration verification plus independent tax monitoring, challenges per-active-developer unit economics at $600/month gross, and checks the design against the three gates plus the full post-launch metric set rather than payout volume and take revenue alone.
expectations: Flags that automatic tax calculation with no active registration in a jurisdiction returns no error and silently collects zero tax
States that under-collected past transactions cannot be retroactively corrected
Requires verifying active tax registrations jurisdiction by jurisdiction rather than trusting that calculation is switched on
Requires monitoring tax collection as its own system, because payout health does not reveal tax health
Challenges the per-active-developer unit economics: roughly $90 a month collected at 15% of $600 gross must be netted against flat per-account and per-payout rail fees plus processing
States unit economics must be modeled per active developer rather than per transaction
Checks that the merchant-of-record posture is stated per app population with tax, chargeback, and payout ownership each explicitly assigned and no transaction type left ambiguous
Checks that every fee instrument names its collection mechanism, its enforcement pair, and its notice commitment in writing
Checks that the published developer docs state the end-to-end sale-to-bank timeline and the jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction tax split

Extends the dashboard beyond payout volume and take revenue to include net take revenue against billing-ops cost, median sale-to-bank days against the published timeline, dispute and chargeback rate attributed to whoever the posture assigned it, waiver coverage among eligible developers, tax-registration coverage of transaction volume, and circumvention incidents
Says to baseline against the platform's own first quarter rather than treating other platforms' published figures as targets

evals.prompt: We have 180 apps already billing our customers directly on their own processors, some of them on three-year contracts signed last year. On January 1 we become merchant of record for everything: single cutover, no exceptions, all 180 migrate. We also want to pull roughly $4M of annual off-marketplace revenue from private deals our partners closed outside the directory onto the marketplace. We have two people on billing engineering and no dedicated compliance headcount. Poke holes.
evals.expected_output: A run that rejects the single cutover for a population under multi-year contracts, names the configurable-per-app posture and its doubled cost against the stated headcount, frames the developer-billed branch as a closing legacy path, and uses the $4M back-book to promote differential-rate migration incentives under the notice commitment.
expectations: Challenges the single-cutover assumption for a legacy population that cannot migrate in one cycle, given the multi-year customer contracts already signed
Names the configurable-per-app posture, running both merchant-of-record postures at once, as what a phased migration actually requires
States its real cost: two billing branches, two tax postures, two payout systems, and doubled developer documentation
Notes the compliance review runs twice under the configurable posture, and flags the two-person billing team with no compliance headcount as the binding effort ceiling
Requires the developer-billed branch to be framed as a closing legacy path with a stated end direction, never as an option offered to new developers
Identifies the roughly $4M off-marketplace back-book as what promotes migration incentives from the starved rung
States that with no measurable back-book the migration-incentive shape should be deleted from the menu rather than parked at the bottom of it
Proposes differential rates as the migration lever, pairing an accelerated benefit on the preferred path with a deferred increase on the legacy one, rather than only waiving fees
Notes the differential-rate lever is worth more than the waived fees themselves
Requires the rate changes involved to run under the published notice commitment, with the unfavorable leg deferred
